location: p. 9 (pdf p. 10), Section 3 'A New Smoothness Measurement', eq. (3.9)
sentence: When f' = 0, we have IS_k = (13/12) (f'' h^2)^2 (1 + O(h^2)), k = 0, 1, 2 (3.9) which implies that the weights resulting from the measurement (3.1) are also 5th order accurate at critical points.

scheme.definition: Fifth-order (r = 3) finite difference WENO scheme. Numerical flux hat f_{j+1/2} = sum_{k=0}^{r-1} omega_k q^r_k(f_{j+k-r+1}, ..., f_{j+k}) (2.10), with q^r_k the r-th order candidate-stencil approximations (2.8). Weights omega_k = alpha_k / (alpha_0 + ... + alpha_{r-1}) (2.15), alpha_k = C^r_k / (epsilon + IS_k)^p (2.16), optimal weights C^3_0 = 1/10, C^3_1 = 6/10, C^3_2 = 3/10 (Table 2); epsilon is a positive real number introduced to avoid a zero denominator (epsilon = 10^-6 in the paper's tests), p = 2 in all tests. New smoothness measurement IS_k = sum_{l=1}^{r-1} int_{x_{j-1/2}}^{x_{j+1/2}} h^{2l-1} (q_k^{(l)})^2 dx (3.1), which for r = 3 gives IS_0 = (13/12)(f_{j-2} - 2f_{j-1} + f_j)^2 + (1/4)(f_{j-2} - 4f_{j-1} + 3f_j)^2 (3.2), IS_1 = (13/12)(f_{j-1} - 2f_j + f_{j+1})^2 + (1/4)(f_{j-1} - f_{j+1})^2 (3.3), IS_2 = (13/12)(f_j - 2f_{j+1} + f_{j+2})^2 + (1/4)(3f_j - 4f_{j+1} + f_{j+2})^2 (3.4).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Smooth region; f' = f'(u_j) = 0 at the point (a critical point of f(u(x))).
Fifth-order accuracy of the weights is understood via the sufficient condition IS_k = D(1 + O(h^{r-1})) for k = 0, ..., r-1 with D a nonzero quantity independent of k.
epsilon = 10^-6 and p = 2 in the tests.
hypotheses.location: p. 6, after (2.16) (epsilon); p. 8, end of Section 2 (p = 2)

justification: Alone: the sentence asserts the expansion (3.9) for all three stencils and that it makes the weights fifth-order accurate at critical points. Henrick, Aslam and Powers (2005) expand the same indicators (their eq. (37) is JS (3.2)-(3.4)) and find a (Dx)^5 term -(13/6) f''f''' + ... in beta_0 and beta_2 (eq. (38)), so at f' = 0 one has beta_0, beta_2 = (13/12)(f''Dx^2)^2 (1 + O(Dx)) (Table 1, p. 552), not 1 + O(Dx^2); hence omega_k = omega-bar_k + O(Dx) near critical points (eq. (39)), and they verify third order at the critical point of f(x) = x^3 + cos(x) with epsilon = 10^-40 (Table 3, p. 555). So (3.9) is false whenever f''' is nonzero at the critical point, and the implication drawn from it fails. With hypotheses: the stated hypotheses (smooth f, f' = 0, condition (2.17)) do not exclude f''' != 0, and the expansion error is pure algebra, so FALSE. Caveat: for a fixed epsilon > 0 (JS use 10^-6), HAP Section 4.3 and Table 3 show epsilon eventually dominates the indicators and the scheme tends to the central scheme as Dx -> 0, so the asymptotic order of the full scheme can still be five for fixed epsilon; that is for a different reason than (3.9), and the sentence's own claim (the expansion and its consequence via (2.17)) is what is refuted.

refutation.source: A. K. Henrick, T. D. Aslam and J. M. Powers, Mapped weighted essentially non-oscillatory schemes: achieving optimal order near critical points, J. Comput. Phys. 207 (2005) 542-567.
refutation.location: p. 552, Section 4.2, after eq. (39) (also Abstract, p. 542; Table 1, p. 552; Table 3, p. 555)
refutation.quote: One should note the discrepancy between the b0 and b2 in Table 1 and those reported in [1, Eqs. (3.5), (3.7) and (3.9)].

sentence: Our new schemes are of uniform order of accuracy r.

scheme.definition: ENO schemes in the abstract form v^{n+1} = A_h . E(tau) . R(.; v^n) (1.10): (i) reconstruction v_h(x, t_n + 0) = R(x; v^n), an essentially non-oscillatory piecewise polynomial reconstruction of order r from cell averages using an adaptive stencil of r + 1 points (1.14a); (ii) solution in the small v_h(., t) = E(t - t_n) v_h(., t_n + 0) for t_n <= t < t_n + tau (1.14b); (iii) cell averaging v_j^{n+1} = (1/h) int_{x_{j-1/2}}^{x_{j+1/2}} v_h(x, t_{n+1} - 0) dx (1.14c). Equivalent conservation form v_j^{n+1} = v_j^n - lambda (fbar_{j+1/2} - fbar_{j-1/2}) (1.16a) with fbar_{j+1/2} = (1/tau) int_0^tau f(v_h(x_{j+1/2}, t_n + eta)) d eta (1.16b). Displayed formulas are partly garbled in the OCR; this is what the prose states.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Accuracy is measured by the local truncation error in the sense of cell averages, (1.8); away from discontinuities and from points where the coefficient e(x) in (1.9a) fails to be Lipschitz continuous, this local truncation error is O(h^{r+1}).

u(x, t) is a smooth solution, the refinement is h -> 0 with tau = O(h), and the numerical approximation is supposed to converge pointwise to u; if e(x) is globally Lipschitz continuous the authors 'expect the cumulative error to be O(h^r)'.
'r-th order accurate' in quotation marks means r-th order in the L1 norm but only (r-1)-th order in the maximum norm, because e(x) may fail to be Lipschitz at isolated points.
For h sufficiently small there are at least r + 1 points of smoothness between discontinuities.

justification: Alone: a careful reader takes 'of uniform order of accuracy r' to mean the computed solution converges at order r for smooth data. Shu (1990), re-testing the degeneracy found by Rogerson and Meiburg, reports for u_t + u_x = 0 with smooth periodic data u0 = sin^4(pi x) that third-order ENO with exact time evolution has an asymptotic L1 order of about 2.5 (pdf p. 7, Fig. 4a), that the original cell-averaged ENO schemes of this paper behave the same ('We have not observed essential differences', p. 3), and that the degeneracy is present for all orders up to seven (p. 4). Hence FALSE. With hypotheses: the paper defines accuracy through the local truncation error in the cell-average sense and only 'expects' an O(h^r) cumulative error under an assumption (e(x) globally Lipschitz) that it cannot check for the adaptive stencil; Shu (1990, p. 1) himself calls the order 'formally uniform high order of accuracy, measured by local truncation errors'. Under the truncation-error reading the sentence may be true; the refutation concerns the global error and is numerical evidence, not a proof. So UNSURE. Weak pair: the contradiction depends on reading 'order of accuracy' as the convergence rate.

refutation.source: C.-W. Shu, Numerical experiments on the accuracy of ENO and modified ENO schemes, NASA CR-182083, ICASE Report No. 90-55, August 1990; published in J. Sci. Comput. 5 (1990) 127-149.

refutation.quote: ENO schemes may lose the full high order accuracy predicted by local truncation error analysis, for scalar linear conservation laws with smooth initial conditions.

sentence: Consequently the numerical solution does not converge to the true solution for any time step.

scheme.definition: WENO5 spatial discretization du_j/dt = -(1/Dx)[(hat f^+_{j+1/2} - hat f^+_{j-1/2}) + (hat f^-_{j+1/2} - hat f^-_{j-1/2})] (2.9), with hat f^+_{j+1/2} = w_0^+ ((2/6)f^+_{j-2} - (7/6)f^+_{j-1} + (11/6)f^+_j) + w_1^+ (-(1/6)f^+_{j-1} + (5/6)f^+_j + (2/6)f^+_{j+1}) + w_2^+ ((2/6)f^+_j + (5/6)f^+_{j+1} - (1/6)f^+_{j+2}) (2.8), Jiang-Shu weights w_k = alpha_k / (alpha_0 + alpha_1 + alpha_2) (2.7) built from smoothness indicators (2.3)-(2.6), and Lax-Friedrichs flux splitting (for u_t = -u_x: f^+ = u, f^- = 0). Time stepping by forward Euler: u_j^{n+1} = u_j^n - (Dt/Dx) L(u_{j-3}^n, ..., u_{j+2}^n) (3.5).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Preceding sentence: 'First we show that the forward Euler method is linearly unstable when coupled with WENO5; i.e., the corresponding CFL number is 0.'

Linear stability analysis: linearize and freeze coefficients, scalar advection u_t = -u_x, CFL number sigma = Dt/Dx; periodic boundary conditions; von Neumann analysis with a single Fourier mode u_j = u-hat e^{i j phi}; linear instability means that for any sigma > 0 there is a phi with |g| > 1.
hypotheses.location: Section 3, pp. 5-7, and proof of Theorem 3.1

hypotheses.hypothesis: Smooth exact solution, so that the weights satisfy w_0 = 1/10 + eps_1, w_1 = 6/10 + eps_2, w_2 = 3/10 + eps_3 with eps_i = O((Dx)^2) (3.2).
Non-convergence is inferred from linear instability ('because they are linearly unstable, these combined methods are not convergent').

justification: Alone: 'for any time step' includes time steps that shrink faster than Dx. Motamed, Macdonald and Ruuth (2010) use the same linearization (frozen WENO5 weights, linear advection, periodic BCs) but test only the N + 1 Fourier modes present on the grid; for forward Euler they obtain linear stability for Dt <= (8 pi^4/15) Dx^5 ~ 51.95 Dx^5 (p. 12), and with the fully nonlinear WENO5 and FE at Dt = 50 Dx^5 they find the computation stable (Section 4.1.1, pp. 17-18). Their Remark 1 (p. 10) shows the spectrum Re z = (7/60) theta^6 near the origin is the same one Wang and Spiteri derive in (3.11). So the sentence, read literally, is FALSE as far as linear stability goes. With hypotheses: Wang and Spiteri's notion of linear stability holds the CFL number sigma = Dt/Dx fixed and lets phi range over a continuum; for every fixed sigma > 0 the scheme is indeed unstable on fine enough grids, and MMR's bound is consistent with that (it forces sigma -> 0). MMR do not state a convergence result or say that Wang and Spiteri were wrong; convergence along Dt ~ Dx^5 would follow for the linearized scheme from stability plus consistency (Lax-Richtmyer), which is my inference, and nothing we read settles it for nonlinear WENO5. So UNSURE. Weak pair: the disagreement is largely about which refinement paths count.

refutation.source: M. Motamed, C. B. Macdonald and S. J. Ruuth, On the linear stability of the fifth-order WENO discretization, Oxford Centre for Collaborative Applied Mathematics Report 10/42 (2010); published in J. Sci. Comput. 47 (2011) 127-149.
refutation.location: Section 5 'Conclusion', p. 26 (pdf p. 28); time-step bound in Section 3.3.1, p. 12; numerical test in Section 4.1.1, pp. 17-18
refutation.quote: In particular, we have shown that the combination of WENO5 with the forward Euler and second-order Runge–Kutta methods is linearly stable provided very small time step-sizes are taken.

sentence: ENO schemes are uniformly high order accurate right up to the shock and are very robust to use.

scheme.definition: ENO schemes as cited: the cell-averaged ENO schemes of Harten, Engquist, Osher and Chakravarthy [5] and the flux version of Shu and Osher on which the paper builds; Section 2 of the paper reviews the finite difference flux version, in which the numerical flux hat f_{j+1/2} is the r-th order approximation q^r_k on one candidate stencil chosen adaptively by comparing undivided differences. Not given as a single formula in the sentence's context.

hypotheses.hypothesis: No hypothesis is stated with the sentence (no smoothness class, norm, time dependence or shock motion).

justification: Alone: read as a statement about the error of the computed solution, it fails. Casper and Carpenter (1995) apply a fourth-order cell-averaged ENO scheme (ENO-4-3, built on the HEOC reconstruction) to a sound wave hitting a shock in quasi-1D Euler flow; measuring L-infinity errors on subdomains away from the shock, they find fourth order upstream but only first order downstream (Sound-Shock Interaction section, Table II), and a linear model problem shows the same first-order loss downstream whenever the discontinuity sits inside a cell. A steady shock gave the design order, so the failure is specific to unsteady interactions, but it is a counterexample to 'uniformly ... right up to the shock'. With hypotheses: the paper states none. Read as a statement about the reconstruction or the local truncation error near the shock (as in Shu's 1997 notes, 'ENO reconstruction is uniformly high order accurate right up to the discontinuity'), it can be true. Which reading is meant is not settled by what we read, so UNSURE. The refutation is numerical. Timing: the NASA TM is dated December 1995, two months after this ICASE report (journal versions later).

refutation.source: J. Casper and M. H. Carpenter, Computational considerations for the simulation of shock-induced sound, NASA Technical Memorandum 110222, NASA Langley Research Center, December 1995.
refutation.location: Abstract; and section 'Sound-Shock Interaction' (discussion of Fig. 4 and Table II)
refutation.quote: However, in an unsteady test case, only first-order results are obtained downstream of a sound-shock interaction.
